Second Chechen War: Russia. Russian authorities were quick to blame Chechens for the bombings, although no Chechen, field commander or otherwise, took responsibility for the attacks.

Battle of Blenheim: Germany. The overwhelming Allied victory ensured the safety of Vienna from the Franco-Bavarian army, thus preventing the collapse of the reconstituted Grand Alliance.

University of Texas tower shooting: United States. The University of Texas tower shooting was a mass shooting that occurred on August 1, 1966, at the University of Texas at Austin.
In which country is OECD based?

In which country was Kamakura shogunate?

Alawi dynasty: Arabic. The dynasty rose to power in the 17th century, beginning with Mawlay al-Sharif who was declared sultan of the Tafilalt in 1631.

Abdul-Malik al-Houthi (born 22 May 1979) is a Yemeni politician and religious leader who is the second leader of the Houthis (Ansar Allah), an organization principally made up of Zaydi Shia Muslims, since 2004.
Fill in the blank: “____ (born 16 February 1983) is a Galician publicist and political activist.”
Alejandra Silva (born 16 February 1983) is a Galician publicist and political activist.
Elected in a surprise 2015 upset over the incumbent, who served as Poland's president from 2015 to 2025 after earlier serving in both the national and European parliaments?
Andrzej Duda (born 16 May 1972) is a Polish lawyer and politician who served as the 6th president of Poland from 2015 to 2025.
Blending cultural nationalism with political moderation, this poet and BJP co-founder served as India's PM from 1998 to 2004 after a brief two-week stint in 1996 — who is he?
Atal Bihari Vajpayee (25 December 1924 - 16 August 2018) was an Indian statesman and a poet who served as the prime minister of India, from 1998 to 2004, and previously for two weeks in 1996.

Grandson of the ninth U.S. president and great-grandson of a Founding Father, this Indianapolis attorney and Union veteran unseated incumbent Grover Cleveland to win the White House in 1888 — who was he?
Benjamin Harrison (August 20, 1833 - March 13, 1901) was the 23rd president of the United States, serving from 1889 to 1893.
This Finnish military commander led the Whites during his country's 1918 civil war, later commanded its armed forces through WWII, and became president from 1944 to 1946 — who is he?
Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim (Finland) was a Finnish military commander and statesman.

Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire

End of World War II in Europe

This mayor of Istanbul since 2019 was suspended from office in 2025 and held in prison pending legal proceedings he calls politically motivated — who is he?
Ekrem İmamoğlu (born 4 June 1970) is a Turkish politician who has served as the 32nd Mayor of Istanbul since 2019.

Founded in Turkey in 2001 after its predecessor was banned by the Constitutional Court, this Islamist political movement split from the group that also produced the AKP, and regularly accuses Erdoğan of undermining democracy — which movement?
Felicity Party is an Islamist political party in Turkey. It was founded in 2001, and is mainly supported by conservative Muslims in Turkey.
He famously graduated dead last in his West Point class in 1861, yet rose fast as a Civil War cavalry commander before the Indian Wars — which officer was he?
George Armstrong Custer (December 5, 1839 - June 25, 1876) was a United States Army officer and cavalry commander in the American Civil War and the American Indian Wars.

King of Sweden from 1611 to 1632, he is credited with the country's rise as a European power and led its military into the Thirty Years' War, shaping Europe's political and religious balance — name this king?
This Olympian herald of ancient Greek mythology wore winged sandals, guided souls to the afterlife as a psychopomp, and served as messenger between the mortal and divine worlds - name the god?
Hermes (Ancient) is an Olympian deity in ancient Greek religion and mythology considered the herald of the gods.

He joined the King's African Rifles as a cook in 1946, then climbed the ranks until he could seize Uganda's presidency in a 1971 coup — whose eight brutal years in power ended with an ill-fated war on Tanzania?
Idi Amin (30 May 1928 - 16 August 2003) was a Ugandan military officer and politician who seized and held power as the third president of Uganda from 1971 until his overthrow in 1979.
Before three famous Pacific voyages, this navigator first surveyed and mapped the entrance to the St. Lawrence River during the Siege of Quebec — who was he?

James Cook (7 November 1728 - 14 February 1779) was a British Royal Navy officer, explorer, and cartographer who led three voyages of exploration to the Pacific and Southern Oceans between 1768 and 1779.

This Royal Navy explorer survived the Napoleonic Wars and two Arctic expeditions, but vanished on a third attempt at the Northwest Passage when his ships froze fast off King William Island — who was he?
John Franklin (16 April 1786 - 11 June 1847) was a British Royal Navy officer, explorer and colonial administrator.
Though a career scholar and government official during Korea's Goryeo period, this military commander is best remembered for his victories in the Third Goryeo-Khitan War — who was he?
Kang Kamch'an (22 December 948 - 9 September 1031) was a medieval Korean government official and military commander during the early days of the Goryeo period (918-1392).
A rival of Hitler for power, this former Reichswehr leader and Weimar-era chancellor was killed in the 1934 purge known as the Night of the Long Knives — who was he?
Kurt von Schleicher (7 April 1882 - 30 June 1934) was a German military officer and the penultimate chancellor of Germany during the Weimar Republic.
Known as 'the Prudent,' this King of France reigned from 1461 to 1483 after rebelling against his father Charles VII in the failed revolt known as the Praguerie — which monarch is this?
Louis XI (3 July 1423 - 30 August 1483), called the Prudent, was King of France from 1461 to 1483.
Serving as First Mayor of Düsseldorf from 2008 to 2014, this FDP politician went on to chair Germany's Bundestag Defence Committee and later joined the European Parliament — who is she?
Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann (ne Jahn; born 10 March 1958) is a German politician of the Free Democratic Party (FDP) who has been serving as a Member of the European Parliament since July 2024.

At Villers-Bocage in June 1944, this German Tiger-tank commander wrecked up to 14 tanks and 15 personnel carriers in a single 15-minute ambush, becoming a postwar 'panzer ace' cult figure — who was he?
Michael Wittmann (22 April 1914 - 8 August 1944) was a German Waffen-SS tank commander during the Second World War.
A former schoolmaster who became India's Defence Minister, this politician served ten terms in his state's legislative assembly and seven in the national Lok Sabha — who is he?
Mulayam Singh Yadav (22 November 1939 - 10 October 2022) was an Indian politician, schoolmaster, lecturer and a socialist figure and the founder of the Samajwadi Party.
Exiled to Onega in 1910 before escaping abroad to meet Lenin and Trotsky, this Bolshevik theorist was active in Soviet government until his 1937 purge — who is he?
Nikolai Bukharin was Soviet revolutionary and politician (1888–1938).
Also called the Old Stone Age, this vast era of human prehistory spans from the earliest known stone tools some 3.3 million years ago to the end of the last ice age — name the period?
Paleolithic is a period in human prehistory distinguished by the original development of stone tools.

In the Hebrew Bible and the Quran, this figure married to an Egyptian guard captain falsely accused Joseph of attempted assault after he rejected her advances, leading to his imprisonment. Who is she?
Potiphar's wife (zoo-), is a figure in the Hebrew Bible and the Quran. The story of Yusuf and Zulaikha is a popular one in Islamic literature.
Hitler called him "the man with the iron heart" — this SS official chaired the Reich Security Main Office and was a principal architect of the Holocaust; who was he?
Reinhard Heydrich (7 March 1904 - 4 June 1942) was a high-ranking SS and police official in Nazi Germany as well as one of the principal architects of the Holocaust.
This royal served as Emir of Kuwait from 2006 until his death in 2020, the fourth son of a previous sheikh who shared part of his name — who was he?
Sabah Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah (16 June 1929 - 29 September 2020) was the Emir of Kuwait from 24 January 2006 until his death in 2020.
After serving as prime minister under Islam Karimov, this leader became his country's second president in 2016 and later chaired the Organization of Turkic States — who is he?
Shavkat Mirziyoyev (born 24 July 1957) is an Uzbek politician who has served as the second president of Uzbekistan since 2016.

A former professor of Mathematical Economics at IIT Delhi, this Indian politician and statistician served as a Cabinet Minister under PM Chandra Shekhar and later chaired a commission on labour standards under PM Narasimha Rao — who is he?
Subramanian Swamy (born 15 September 1939) is an Indian politician, economist and statistician.

This British Labour politician spent 47 of 51 years as an MP and later led the Stop the War Coalition — though for three years he had to be styled The Viscount Stansgate after inheriting his father's title. Who was he?

Tony Benn (3 April 1925 - 14 March 2014), known between 1960 and 1963 as The Viscount Stansgate, was a British Labour Party politician and political activist who served as a Cabinet minister in the 1960s and 1970s.

Likely descended from a group that entered the Roman Empire in 376 and later defeated Roman forces at Adrianople, this Gothic people united under Alaric the First, sacked Rome itself in 410, and founded a kingdom at Toulouse — name this people?
Visigoths were a Gothic people who emerged in the Balkans during late antiquity.

Relocated to San Francisco as a child under a federal urbanization program, this activist joined the Occupation of Alcatraz and became the first woman elected Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation — who was she?
Wilma Mankiller (November 18, 1945 - April 6, 2010) was a Native American activist, social worker, community developer and the first woman elected to serve as Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation.
This uprising ended the Qing dynasty's 267-year reign and more than two thousand years of imperial rule in China, ushering in the country's republican era. What is it called?
1911 Revolution: End of Qing dynasty in China. The revolution was the culmination of a decade of agitation, revolts, and uprisings.

Founded in 1912 to oppose oppression of Black South Africans, this liberation movement has governed the country since 1994's first post-apartheid election, when Nelson Mandela became president — which party?
African National Congress: Political party in South Africa.

Amon Göth: Austrian military officer and war criminal (1908–1946)

Antonio Inoki: Japanese wrestler and politician (1943–2022)

Augustus II the Strong: King of Poland, Elector of Saxony and Grand Duke of Lithuania (1670–1733)
In 1575, the combined forces of Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu crushed the Takeda clan's cavalry, effectively securing Nobunaga's unification of Japan — what clash was this?
Battle of Nagashino: 1575 Oda-Tokugawa victory over the Takeda clan.

Cambodian Civil War: 1967–1975 conflict in Cambodia.

Becoming heir to the Habsburg throne after his uncle Archduke Franz Ferdinand's assassination in 1914, this monarch ruled a central European empire from 1916 until its dissolution in 1918, having secretly sought peace with the Allies during the war — who was he?
Charles I of Austria: Habsburg monarch from 1916 to 1918. Charles succeeded to the thrones in November 1916 following the death of his grand-uncle, Franz Joseph.
The longest-serving leader of the Labour Party, this British statesman was deputy prime minister under Churchill before becoming PM himself in 1945?
Clement Attlee: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1945 to 1951.
This Swedish diplomat became the youngest UN Secretary-General ever at 47, oversaw creation of the UN's first peacekeeping forces in Egypt and the Congo, and died in a 1961 plane crash — who was he?
Dag Hammarskjöld: UN Secretary-General from 1953 to 1961.
Becoming chief minister at just 44 — the second-youngest in his state's history — this Indian politician is now serving his third term leading Maharashtra — who is he?
Devendra Fadnavis: 18th Chief Minister of Maharashtra (2014-2019; since 2024)
This book of Hebrew wisdom literature opens with 'Vanity of vanities! All is futile!', its main body voiced by a speaker called Kohelet — which book of the Bible?
Ecclesiastes: Book of the Hebrew Bible (450–180 BCE)
An Islamic scholar and Sufi who unexpectedly found himself commanding tribal fighters, he held off French colonial forces in Algiers for seventeen years before surrendering in 1847 — who was he?
Emir Abdelkader: Algerian religious and military leader (1808–1883)
Married to Saudi Arabia's king in 1984, this royal spouse is the mother of the crown prince and five other princes — who is she?
Fahda bint Falah Al Hithlain: Third wife of King Salman of Saudi Arabia.
Founded by the Italian saint Francis of Assisi, this Catholic religious family includes the Order of Friars Minor for men and the Order of Saint Clare for nuns — what are its members called?
Franciscans: Group of religious orders within the Catholic Church connected with St. Francis of Assisi.

In January 2021, Reddit's r/wallstreetbets drove the stock of an American video game retailer up nearly 30-fold in a single month, inflicting massive losses on the hedge funds betting against it. What is this market event known as?
GameStop short squeeze: 2021 financial markets event.
The longest-serving Philippine president since Marcos, she first broke ground as the country's first female vice president before leading the nation from 2001 to 2010. Who is she?

Gloria Macapagal Arroyo: President of the Philippines from 2001 to 2010. Estrada was ousted by the Second EDSA Revolution in 2001, and Arroyo was sworn in as president by Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr. on January 20.

Ruled by a dynasty once known as the House of Austria, this 1516–1700 European empire commanded territory stretching from the Americas to the Philippines and briefly folded in Portugal — what's this historical era called?
Habsburg Spain: Period of Spanish history (1516–1700)

Often depicted holding twin torches and accompanied by dogs, this Greek goddess of crossroads, night, and magic first appears in Hesiod's 'Theogony' and was worshipped in Athens as a protector of the household — who is she?
Hecate: Greek goddess of magic and transitions. The earliest evidence for Hecate's cult comes from Selinunte, in Sicily.
Also known as Brahmanism, this ancient belief system of Indo-Aryan peoples in Punjab and the western Ganges plain (c. 1500-500 BCE) gave rise to today's Hinduism — what was it called?
Historical Vedic religion: 1500–500 BC Indo-Aryan religious practices of northwest India.
Founded in Leipzig in 1984 and now based in Zürich, which organization chronicles the history and statistics of association football despite having no official affiliation with FIFA?
IFFHS: Organisation chronicling the history and records of association football.
This political ideology holds that Islam should shape government and society through the implementation of sharia and pan-Islamic unity — what is it called?

Son of Mary, Queen of Scots, this king took the Scottish throne in infancy in 1567 and united it in personal union with England's in 1603 — though the two kingdoms kept separate parliaments. Who was he?
James VI and I: King of Scotland from 1567 to 1625, King of England and Ireland from 1603.
A Catalan lawyer-turned-club president, he steered his team to a record six trophies in twelve months back in 2009 and returned to the presidency again in 2021 — who is he?

The eldest of nine children born into a family with presidential ambitions, this Navy pilot died in 1944 flying a secret mission called Operation Aphrodite, redirecting his father's hopes to his younger brother — who was he?
Joseph P. Kennedy Jr.: American naval aviator (1915–1944)
Fought between India and Pakistan from May to July 1999 high in the mountains of Ladakh along the Line of Control, this clash was code-named Operation Vijay by India — what is it known as?
Kargil War: 1999 conflict between India and Pakistan. It also marks one of only two instances of conventional warfare between nuclear-armed states (alongside the Sino-Soviet border conflict).
Established in 1832 after the War of Independence, this monarchy survived on and off — including a 1935 restoration — until its final abolition in 1973. What was this Hellenic state called?
Kingdom of Greece: Period of Greek statehood from 1832 to 1923 and 1935 to 1973.
This Colorado congresswoman once ran Shooters Grill in Rifle, where staff were encouraged to carry firearms openly, before her 2020 upset of five-term incumbent Scott Tipton — who is she?

Once president of the Oxford University Liberal Democrats, this British politician later became the shortest-serving prime minister in her country's history, stepping down on her fiftieth day. Who is she?
Liz Truss: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom in 2022.
Serving as King Louis XV's official chief mistress from 1745, this Frenchwoman later became the queen's thirteenth lady-in-waiting and a major patron of the arts — who is she?
Madame de Pompadour: Chief mistress of Louis XV (1721–1764)
A chemistry graduate turned barrister, this stateswoman became Britain's first woman prime minister and earned the nickname the 'Iron Lady' — who is she?
Margaret Thatcher: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990.
A civil engineer turned centre-right businessman-politician, he ran Buenos Aires before serving as Argentina's president from 2015 to 2019. Who is he?

Mauricio Macri: President of Argentina from 2015 to 2019. Mauricio Macri ([mawˈɾisjo ˈmakɾi]; born 8 February 1959) is an Argentine businessman and politician who served as President of Argentina from 2015 to 2019.

Serving as the Soviet Union's largely ceremonial head of state from 1919 to 1946 while real power sat with Stalin, this former metalworker had been mayor of Petrograd after the October Revolution — who was he?
Grand Duke Michael Alexandrovich of Russia
Often depicted as King Arthur's sister, this ambiguous enchantress from medieval legend could be portrayed as either a healing fairy or a dangerous sorceress — who is she?

Morgan le Fay: Enchantress in the Arthurian legend. A significant aspect in many of Morgan's medieval and later iterations is the unpredictable duality of her nature, with potential for both good and evil.
After two failed attempts in 1944, this Hindu nationalist activist shot Mahatma Gandhi three times at a Delhi prayer meeting in January 1948 — who was he?
Nathuram Godse: Assassin of Mahatma Gandhi (1910–1949)

Known as "King Father," this royal led Cambodia through French rule, independence, a republic, the Khmer Rouge years and back to monarchy — serving as King, Chief of State and Prime Minister. Who was he?
Of Junker landowner stock, this 'Iron Chancellor' practiced Realpolitik and engineered the unification of Germany, becoming its first chancellor in 1871 — who is he?
Otto von Bismarck: Chancellor of Germany from 1871 to 1890.
Twice imprisoned during a 1920s satyagraha protest, this Indian activist quit the Congress party in 1925 and went on to found the movement behind modern Dravidian politics. Who is he?
Periyar: Indian social activist and politician (1879–1973)

After eight years in UN-funded public health work, this Indian strategist helped re-elect Narendra Modi as Gujarat's chief minister in 2012 before founding his own party ahead of the 2025 Bihar election — who is he?
Prashant Kishor: Indian politician. Prashant Kishor (born 20 March 1977), colloquially known as PK, is an Indian politician, the founder of the Jan Suraaj Party and a former political strategist.

Serving as India's president from 2017 to 2022, he was the first person from Uttar Pradesh and the first member of the Bharatiya Janata Party to hold that office, after serving as Governor of Bihar — who is he?
Ram Nath Kovind: President of India from 2017 to 2022.

Fought from 1921 to 1926, this conflict pitted Spain and later France against Berber guerrillas led by Abd el-Krim in northern Morocco, and saw history's first amphibious landing to use tanks and aircraft — which conflict?
Rif War: 1921–1926 war between Spain and Riffian tribes of Morocco.
From 1904 to 1905, two empires clashed over rival ambitions in Manchuria and Korea, fighting major naval battles in the Yellow Sea and the Sea of Japan — which war was this?
Russo-Japanese War: 1904–1905 conflict in East Asia.
Renowned in the Book of Genesis for her hospitality and beauty, this matriarch was the wife of Abraham and mother of Isaac — who is she?
Sarah: Biblical matriarch. Sarah (originally Sarai) is a biblical matriarch, prophet, and major figure in Abrahamic religions.
In the Book of Revelation, these divine horn blasts — sounded one at a time by angels after the breaking of the final seal — unleash a series of apocalyptic disasters. What are they called?
Seven trumpets: Described in the Book of Revelation. The seven trumpets are sounded by seven angels and the events that follow are described in detail in Revelation 8–11.

Prince Arthur, Duke of Connaught and Strathearn
Younger brother of a U.S. president and an attorney general, he represented Massachusetts in the Senate from 1962 until his death in 2009 — which long-serving senator?
Ted Kennedy: American lawyer and politician (1932–2009)
This retired Royal Navy vice admiral served as an equerry to Queen Elizabeth II before marrying her only daughter in 1992 — who is he?
Timothy Laurence: Retired Royal Navy officer (born 1955)
Explicitly authorized by the Constitution, this independent government agency replaced a Cabinet department in 1971 and holds a legal monopoly on traditional letter delivery — which agency?
United States Postal Service: Independent agency of the U.S. federal government.
Born in Leningrad and working 16 years as a KGB foreign intelligence officer, this politician has served as the de facto Russian leader since 1999 — who is he?
Vladimir Putin: President of Russia (2000–2008; since 2012)
Among Queen Victoria's 42 grandchildren he was the eldest, yet he'd preside over the end of his dynasty's 400-year grip on Prussia when he abdicated in 1918 — which last German Emperor?
Wilhelm II: German Emperor from 1888 to 1918.
Founded by Grigory Yavlinsky and translating to 'Apple' in Russian, this social-liberal party held seats in the State Duma before losing its faction status in 2003 — which party?
Yabloko: Russian political party. The party consequently participated in the elections of deputies of the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation of all eight convocations.

The first woman and youngest person ever to hold Slovakia's presidency, this lawyer and environmental activist won the 2016 Goldman Environmental Prize for fighting a toxic landfill in her hometown. Who is she?
Zuzana Čaputová: President of Slovakia from 2019 to 2024.

Which of these four was born earliest?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Which of these four began earliest?
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Pierre Curie is a physicist. Pierre Curie (15 May 1859 – 19 April 1906) was a French physicist and chemist, and a pioneer in crystallography and magnetism.
Which of these four is a chemist?
Samuel Conway is a chemist. Samuel Charles Conway (born June 4, 1965) is an American researcher in the pharmaceutical, biomedical and agrochemical fields of organic chemistry.
What is the atomic number of Beryllium?
Beryllium is a chemical element; it has symbol Be and atomic number 4.
In what year was Galileo Galilei born?
Galileo Galilei: Galileo has been called the father of observational astronomy, modern-era classical physics, the scientific method, and modern science.
In what year was Caesium discovered?
Caesium (IUPAC spelling; also spelled cesium in American English) is a chemical element; it has symbol Cs and atomic number 55.
In what year was Osmium discovered?
Osmium (from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ) 'smell') is a chemical element; it has symbol Os and atomic number 76.
Which company manufactures AIDC F-CK-1 Ching-kuo?
AIDC F-CK-1 Ching-kuo: Aerospace Industrial Development Corporation. The aircraft made its first flight in 1989.
In which country is Douglas A-4 Skyhawk based?
Douglas A-4 Skyhawk: United States. It was originally designated A4D under the United States Navy's pre-1962 designation system.
Who is credited with discovering Barium?
Barium: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Barium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ba and atomic number 56.
Who is credited with discovering Lawrencium?
Lawrencium: Albert Ghiorso. Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lr (formerly Lw) and atomic number 103.
Who is credited with discovering Francium?
Francium: Marguerite Perey. Francium is a chemical element; it has symbol Fr and atomic number 87.

This alternative-medicine practice, a component of traditional Chinese medicine, involves inserting thin needles into the body, though its underlying theories are considered pseudoscientific by mainstream science — what's the practice called?
Acupuncture is a form of alternative medicine and a component of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) in which thin needles are inserted into the body.
These organic compounds, formed when one or more hydrogens in ammonia are replaced by carbon-based groups, are defined by their carbon-nitrogen bonds — what's this class of compounds called?
Amine (UK also) are organic compounds that contain carbon-nitrogen bonds.
Fill in the blank: “____ (April 21, 1971 - September 30, 2011) was an American-Yemeni Islamic cleric and lecturer.”

Anwar al-Awlaki (April 21, 1971 - September 30, 2011) was an American-Yemeni Islamic cleric and lecturer. Al-Awlaki was the first U.S. citizen to be targeted and assassinated by a U.S. government drone strike.
Originally built by Hawker Siddeley and still produced under license in India today, this subsonic British trainer aircraft equips the Red Arrows aerobatic team — which jet?
BAE Systems Hawk is a British single-engine, subsonic, jet-powered advanced trainer aircraft.
Ranging from fingerprints and iris scans to typing rhythm and the way someone walks, these measurable human traits are used for identification and surveillance — what's the general term for them?
Biometrics are body measurements and calculations related to human characteristics and features.
This American actor played Kyle Parks on Lifetime's The Client List before joining the cast of Revenge as Ben Hunter — who is he?
Brian Hallisay (born October 31, 1978) is an American actor, known for his roles as Will Davis in The CW drama series Privileged and Kyle Parks in the Lifetime drama series The Client List.

This sweet, aromatic orange-fleshed melon goes by different names depending on where you are — 'rockmelon' in Australia and New Zealand, 'spanspek' in Southern Africa — and can weigh up to 5 kilograms. What fruit is this?
Cantaloupe (also spelled cantaloup and cantelope;, or) is a type of true melon (Cucumis melo) with sweet, aromatic, and usually orange flesh.
Its other name is varicella, it spreads through the air, and it tends to hit adults harder than children — which itchy, blister-forming disease is this?
Chickenpox is a highly contagious disease caused by varicella zoster virus (VZV), a member of the herpesvirus family.
Found naturally in the sap of the opium poppy and a prodrug of morphine, which opiate treats mild-to-moderate pain and is often paired with paracetamol?
Codeine is an opiate and prodrug of morphine mainly used to treat pain, coughing, and diarrhea.
Affecting roughly 1 in 22,000 births and more common in girls, which genetic condition caused by a chromosome 5 deletion takes its French name from a feline-sounding cry?
Cri du chat syndrome is a rare genetic disorder due to a partial chromosome deletion on chromosome 5.

In this heart condition, the heart chamber enlarges and loses its ability to pump blood effectively, with causes ranging from genetics and alcohol to certain infections and pregnancy complications — name this condition?
Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a condition in which the heart becomes enlarged and cannot pump blood effectively.

Specializing in legislative process and authoritarian rule, this Russian scholar became a fellow at a Berlin academy and hosts her own political radio talk show, reaching a million YouTube subscribers by 2022 — who is she?
Ekaterina Schulmann (ne Zaslavskaya; born 19 August 1978) is a Russian political scientist specializing in legislative processes and authoritarian governance.
This sweet-tasting but toxic diol is a workhorse of antifreeze and polyester manufacturing, and astronomers have even detected the molecule in space — what is it?
Ethylene glycol (IUPAC name: ethane-1,2-diol) is an organic compound (a vicinal diol) with the formula (CH2OH)2.
This infection and inflammation of hair follicles produces white-tipped pimples anywhere on hair-covered skin, and is considered a distinct condition from acne. Name it?
Folliculitis is the infection and inflammation of one or more hair follicles.
Caught from a tiny waterborne protist and common in travelers and children, it brings fatty, sticky diarrhea and abdominal pain a week or three after exposure — what is this parasitic illness?
Giardiasis is a parasitic disease caused by the protist enteropathogen Giardia duodenalis (also known as G. lamblia).

Rooted in a Hebrew word meaning 'to walk' or 'to go,' this collective body of Jewish religious law guides both worship and everyday life, tracing back to biblical commandments and later rabbinic codes — what is it?
Halakha (hah-), is the collective body of Jewish religious laws that are derived from the Written and Oral Torah.
Before founding his own Italian supercar company, this Argentine-Italian engineer worked for both Renault and Lamborghini — who is he?
Horacio Pagani (auto executive) (born 10 November 1955) is an Argentine-Italian businessman and automobile engineer in the automotive industry.

Native to South China and Vietnam, this evergreen tree produces a star-shaped fruit whose spice tastes like anise, and whose oil a drugmaker relied on until switching to genetically modified E. coli in 2012 — name this tree?
Illicium verum (star anise or badian, Chinese star anise, star anise seed, star aniseed and star of anise) is a medium-sized evergreen tree native to South China and northeast Vietnam.

This Swiss psychologist's theory of cognitive development, paired with his epistemological views, is together known as genetic epistemology, and remains foundational in early-childhood education. Who is he?
Jean Piaget (9 August 1896 - 16 September 1980) was a Swiss psychologist known for his work on child development.
Also called a kilopond, this deprecated gravitational metric unit equals exactly 9.80665 newtons — the weight of a one-thousand-gram mass under standard gravity. What is it?
Kilogram-force (kgf or kgF), or kilopond (kp, from Latin pondus, 'weight'), is a non-standard gravitational metric unit of force equal to the weight on Earth of a one-kilogram mass.
This Soviet theoretical physicist laid the foundations of twentieth-century condensed matter physics and explained the theory behind superfluid helium — who is he?
Lev Landau (22 January 1908 - 1 April 1968) was a Soviet physicist who made fundamental contributions to many areas of theoretical physics.
Over a 55-year career this American botanist bred more than 800 plant varieties, from the Shasta daisy to the Santa Rosa plum and a spineless cactus for cattle — who was he?

Luther Burbank (March 7, 1849 - April 11, 1926) was an American botanist, horticulturist, and pioneer in agricultural science who developed more than 800 strains and varieties of plants over his 55-year career.
In hermaphroditic species this reproductive pairing isn't strictly required, since self-fertilization is possible — what is the general term for it?
Mating refers to the pairing of either opposite-sex or hermaphroditic organisms for the purpose of sexual reproduction.

Usually white but sometimes tinged yellow or pink, this liquid food produced by mammary glands is the primary source of nutrition for young mammals, with its very first production called colostrum — name the substance?
Milk is usually a white liquid food (but can be shades of yellow, cream, pink, or brown) produced by the mammary glands of lactating mammals.
Named from the Ancient Greek for 'mouse's ear' after its foliage's shape, this genus of small blue Northern Hemisphere flowers serves as Alaska's official state flower — what's the genus?
Myosotis is a genus of flowering plants in the borage family Boraginaceae.
Built from nucleotide units of a sugar, a phosphate, and a nitrogenous base, these biomolecules come in two main classes distinguished by whether their sugar is ribose or deoxyribose — what are they?
Nucleic acid are large biomolecules that are crucial in all cells and viruses.
Belonging to the pea family and native to Mesoamerica, this vine produces blue or white flowers and an edible tuberous root known in Spanish as jícama — which species?
Pachyrhizus erosus (from Nahuatl languages: xicamatl) or Mexican turnip, is a native Mesoamerican vine, although the name jicama most commonly refers to the plant's edible tuberous root.
This mammalian skin secretion comes in two types — a watery kind for cooling and an oilier kind found in the armpits that gains odor from bacteria — what is it?
Perspiration is the fluid secreted by sweat glands in the skin of mammals.
Known as greater plantain, this Eurasian-native flowering plant is often confused by name with a banana relative, despite no real botanical connection between the two. Which species is it?
Plantago major is a species of flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae.

Found below the bladder with the urethra passing through it, this male reproductive gland acts as a mechanical switch between urination and ejaculation, and produces fluid that becomes part of semen — name the gland?
Prostate is an accessory gland of the male reproductive system and a muscle-driven mechanical switch between urination and ejaculation.

The largest of the true foxes and the most widely distributed carnivore on Earth, it spread alongside human settlement so successfully that, after being introduced to Australia, it landed on the list of the world's 100 worst invasive species. Which animal is it?
Red fox (Vulpes vulpes) is the largest of the true foxes, and the most widely distributed member of the order Carnivora.
Enforcing memory safety without a garbage collector through something called a 'borrow checker,' this general-purpose language blends functional and object-oriented paradigms — which language?
Rust (programming language) is a general-purpose programming language which emphasizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety.
Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754, this term describes an unplanned fortunate discovery, as with penicillin or the microwave oven — what is it called?
Serendipity is an unplanned fortunate discovery. The concept is often associated with scientific and technological breakthroughs, where accidental discoveries led to new insights or inventions.

Born in the Bronx to Puerto Rican parents and raised by her mother after her father's death, this Princeton grad became the third woman on the U.S. Supreme Court after Barack Obama's 2009 appointment — name this justice?
Sonia Sotomayor (born June 25, 1954) is an American lawyer and jurist who serves as an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States.
This towering perennial grass, native to New Guinea, stores so much natural sweetness in its jointed stalks that it's the world's primary source for a common sweetener — what plant is it?
Sugarcane is a species of tall, perennial grass (in the genus Saccharum, tribe Andropogoneae) that is used for sugar production.
Enhanced by painted scenery and stagecraft like lighting, this live performing art shares its name with the very buildings where its shows are staged — what is it?

Theatre is a collaborative form of performing art that uses live performers, usually actors, to present experiences of a real or imagined event before a live audience in a specific place, often a stage.
Named for the compulsive pulling of one's own hair, this disorder brings a brief positive feeling with each pull but is notoriously hard to stop — what is it?
Trichotillomania (TTM), also known as hair-pulling disorder or compulsive hair pulling, is a mental disorder characterized by a long-term urge that results in the pulling out of one's own hair.
Known also as sight or eyesight, this sense lets the body detect photons and build a picture of its environment using daytime or night modes — what is it?
Visual perception is the ability to detect light and use it to form an image of the surrounding environment.
The first woman ever to serve as Ukraine's prime minister, this politician held that post in 2005 and again from 2007 to 2010, and now leads the Batkivshchyna political party — who is she?

Yulia Tymoshenko (ne Hrihyan; born 27 November 1960) is a Ukrainian politician, who served as Prime Minister of Ukraine in 2005, and again from 2007 until 2010; the first woman in Ukraine to hold that position.
Nicknamed the 'upside-down tree' for its unusual silhouette, this genus of long-lived African and Malagasy giants was named after a French naturalist — what genus is it?
Adansonia: Genus of trees known as baobab.
Made in the adrenal cortex, this hormone tells the kidney to hang onto sodium and dump potassium, quietly steering your blood pressure and blood volume — what is it?
Formed when ammonia gains an extra hydrogen ion, this positively charged molecule, NH4+, is a key player in the global nitrogen cycle — what is it?

Native to the Americas from northern Mexico to northern Argentina, this flowering plant genus is the largest in the arum family and includes types nicknamed flamingo flower and pigtail plant. What genus is it?
Anthurium: Genus of plants. Anthurium (Schott, 1829) is a genus of about 1,000 species of flowering plants, the largest genus of the arum family, Araceae.
These chitin-armored invertebrates must shed their exoskeletons to grow and circulate haemolymph through an open body cavity — and may number up to ten million species. What are they?
Arthropod: Phylum of invertebrates with jointed exoskeletons.
With six species native to Africa (and one also found in Arabia), these large Old World monkeys have dog-like muzzles and have existed for at least two million years — what are they called?

This steel-gray, brittle alkaline earth metal is found naturally only in combination with other elements, making up gemstones like aquamarine and emerald, and bonds so strongly to oxygen that extracting it is notoriously difficult — which element, atomic number 4?
Beryllium: Chemical element with atomic number 4 (Be)

Announced at the 1984 Farnborough Airshow and launched by Northwest Airlines, this advanced wide-body airliner added 6-foot winglets and a stretched upper deck to an already-famous jumbo jet design — which aircraft?
Boeing 747-400: Wide-body airliner, improved production series of the 747.
Its name means 'thunder lizard,' and though long dismissed as just another sauropod genus, a 2015 study restored this dinosaur's status as distinct — which one?
Brontosaurus: Genus of diplodocid sauropod dinosaur. In subsequent years, two more species of Brontosaurus were named: B. parvus in 1902 and B. yahnahpin in 1994.
With more than 220 species and over 26,000 registered cultivars, this flowering plant genus includes the very species whose leaves are processed into tea worldwide — which genus?
Camellia: Genus of flowering plants in the tea family.
A woody shrub native to South America, this starchy tuber yields tapioca and, when grated and toasted, becomes Brazil's farofa and West Africa's garri — what crop is it?
Cassava: Staple crop. Although a perennial plant, cassava is extensively cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions as an annual crop for its edible starchy tuberous root.
Known by the common name 'greater celandine,' this perennial flowering plant belongs to the poppy family and is native to Europe and western Asia — what's its scientific name?
Chelidonium majus: Species of flowering plant in the poppy family. One of two species in the genus Chelidonium, it is native to Europe and western Asia and introduced widely in North America.
A political scientist studying voter turnout and race, this scholar rose through Harvard's deanships to become its 30th president in 2023 — only to resign months later; who is she?
Claudine Gay: American political scientist and university administrator (born 1970)
Declared one of the world's most invasive species in 2000 and named Australia's top pest problem in 2008, which highly adaptable Asian bird thrives in cities?
Common myna: Bird of the family Sturnidae.
Found mainly in muscle and brain tissue, which organic compound helps recycle ATP — its phosphorylated form donating phosphate to ADP to regenerate the body's energy currency?
Creatine: Chemical compound. Creatine ( or) is an organic compound that, in vertebrates, facilitates recycling of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), primarily in muscle and brain tissue.
Also called thornapple or devil's trumpet, this genus of nine highly poisonous nightshade plants lent its American name to an outbreak in colonial Jamestown — what genus is it?
Datura: Genus of poisonous, potentially psychoactive plants.

This colourless, water-mixable lab solvent is technically odorless — but degraded samples reek of fish thanks to a dimethylamine impurity. It's better known by a three-letter abbreviation; what's the compound?
Dimethylformamide: Chemical compound. Dimethylformamide, DMF is an organic compound with the chemical formula HCON(CH3)2.
Of the 68 species bearing this name, only the Aquilinae are genetically "true" ones — the rest just qualify as any bird of prey big enough to hunt sizeable vertebrates; what's the common name?
Eagle: Large bird of prey. Eagle is the common name for certain large birds of prey within the family of the Accipitridae.
Affecting roughly 10% of women of reproductive age — nearly 200 million worldwide — this disease occurs when tissue like the uterine lining grows on the ovaries, bowel, or elsewhere. What is it?

Exercise, laughter, dancing, and romantic love can all trigger this intense state of well-being via the brain's pleasure centers — though it's also a symptom of mania and the lure of addictive drugs. What is it?
Euphoria: Intense feelings of well-being. Euphoria (yoo-FOR-ee-ə) is the experience (or affect) of pleasure or excitement and intense feelings of well-being and happiness.
This German mathematician's 1872 Erlangen program reorganized all of geometry by its underlying symmetry groups, and he later turned Göttingen into a world center of research — who was he?
Named for hindwings that resemble human ears when unfolded, this reddish-brown insect is a common household pest known for the pincers at the tip of its abdomen — which species?
Forficula auricularia: Species of earwig. It is an omnivorous insect belonging to the family Forficulidae.

Marked by heartburn, regurgitation, and even dental corrosion from stomach acid creeping back up the digestive tract, this chronic condition can, if untreated, lead to esophageal stricture or Barrett's esophagus — what is it?
Gastroesophageal reflux disease: Flow of stomach contents into the esophagus.
The most abundant free amino acid in human blood, this one is named after the compound found in gluten and is coded for by the codons CAA and CAG — what is it?
Glutamine: Amino acid. Glutamine (symbol Gln or Q) is an α-amino acid that is used in the biosynthesis of proteins.
Breeders prefer to call it a 'cavy,' and despite its name it hails from the Andes rather than West Africa and isn't related to swine at all — which Andean rodent is it?
Guinea pig: Domesticated rodent from South America.
This medical term describes red blood cells rupturing and spilling their contents into the plasma — a process triggered by bacterial toxins or even intense exercise. What is it?
Hemolysis: Rupturing of red blood cells and release of their contents. Hemolysis may occur in vivo or in vitro.

The only birds whose first two neck vertebrae are fused together, these Old World birds have a long down-curved bill sometimes topped with a bony casque, and share an ecological niche with toucans in the Americas — which birds?
Hornbill: Family of birds. The family is omnivorous, feeding on fruit and small animals.

When the thyroid produces too little hormone, the body slows down — cold intolerance, fatigue, constipation, weight gain — and worldwide too little dietary iodine is the leading cause. What's the condition?
Hypothyroidism: Insufficient production of thyroid hormones.

A functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel movement consistency over long periods, sometimes years, it can negatively affect quality of life and is associated with anxiety and depression. What condition is this?
Irritable bowel syndrome: Functional gastrointestinal disorder. The cause of IBS is not known but multiple factors have been proposed to lead to the condition.
This British chemical engineer founded a major chemicals group in 1998 and later became a minority shareholder with control over football operations at Manchester United — who is he?
Jim Ratcliffe: British engineer and businessman (born 1952)
Its subfamily name literally means 'large foot,' it's native to Australia and New Guinea, and a 2019 government tally counted some 42.8 million of them in harvest areas. Which marsupial?
Kangaroo: Marsupial of the family Macropodidae.
Also called the Mediterranean black widow, this venomous spider is common throughout the Mediterranean region and central Asia — what species is it?

Latrodectus tredecimguttatus: Species of spider. Latrodectus tredecimguttatus, also known as the Mediterranean black widow or the European black widow, is a species in the genus Latrodectus of the widow spiders.
Native to the Indo-Pacific, this venomous aquarium favorite sports red-and-black banded warning colors and ostentatious spiny fins, and has become an invasive nightmare in the Caribbean — what is it?
Named from the Latin for "wolf," this autoimmune disease often announces itself with a red facial rash and alternates between flares and remission — what is it?
Lupus: Autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks healthy tissue.
Boiled down from its sap to make a beloved breakfast syrup, this genus of roughly 132 tree and shrub species counts the sycamore as its type species — which genus of trees?
Nicknamed a 'semi-lunar' cartilage for its half-moon shape, this crescent-shaped structure cushions joints like the knee, wrist, and jaw — what is it?
Meniscus (anatomy): Fibrocartilaginous part of a bone joint.
Based on a Soviet fighter jet but optimized for ground attack, this variable-sweep aircraft was license-built in India as the 'Bahadur,' or 'Valiant' — which jet?
Mikoyan MiG-27: Series of 1970s Soviet attack aircraft.

First identified from skulls found in a Dutch chalk quarry near Maastricht and initially mistaken for crocodile or whale bones, this giant marine lizard genus lived until 66 million years ago — which genus is it?
Mosasaurus: Extinct genus of marine lizard from the Late Cretaceous.
Colloquially known as a moon, this type of astronomical body orbits a planet or dwarf planet, with 455 confirmed examples across the Solar System's six major systems — what is it called?
Natural satellite: Astronomical body that orbits a planet. Natural satellites are colloquially referred to as moons, by analogy with the Moon, Earth's natural satellite.
This American physicist won the 1989 Nobel for inventing the separated oscillatory field method behind atomic clocks, and helped found both Brookhaven National Laboratory and Fermilab — who was he?

Numbering 126 species, these are the largest order of marsupials in the Western Hemisphere — and only one of them, the Virginia variety, made it as far north as the United States and Canada. What animal is this?

Named after the bones that house them — frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid — these four paired air-filled spaces surround the nasal cavity and have a still-debated evolutionary purpose — what are they called?
Paranasal sinuses: Air-filled spaces surrounding the nasal cavity.
This serous membrane lines the abdominal cavity and serves as a conduit for the blood vessels and nerves of the organs it covers — what is it called?
Peritoneum: Membrane that forms lining of abdominal cavity or coelom.

A counting argument in mathematics: if you have more items than containers, at least one container must hold more than one item. Famous example: three gloves, but only two hand categories — what's this principle?
Pigeonhole principle: If there are more items than boxes holding them, one box must contain at least two items.
Looking like a jellyfish but actually a floating colony of cooperating zooids, this venomous siphonophore is also nicknamed the bluebottle — what is it?
Portuguese man o' war: Species of marine cnidarian.

This noncontagious autoimmune disease shows up as dry, scaly red or purple patches, and injuring the skin can trigger new lesions right at that spot — a quirk called the Koebner phenomenon — what is it?
Psoriasis: Autoimmune diseases of the skin. Psoriasis is a long-lasting, noncontagious autoimmune disease characterized by patches of abnormal skin.

Born Richard Alpert, this spiritual teacher researched psychedelics with Timothy Leary at Harvard before writing the 1971 bestseller Be Here Now, popularizing Eastern spirituality in the West. What name did he later take?
As chairman of Purdue Pharma, this physician-businessman oversaw the launch of OxyContin and was later portrayed in the miniseries Dopesick and Painkiller — who is he?
Also called false saffron, this thistle-like annual is one of the world's oldest crops, prized today for the vegetable oil pressed from its seeds — what plant is it?
Safflower: Species of plant. Safflower (Carthamus tinctorius), also false saffron, is a highly branched, herbaceous, thistle-like annual plant in the family Asteraceae.
Co-founder of the file-sharing service Napster, this entrepreneur became Facebook's first president before later founding a philanthropic foundation focused on life sciences — who is he?
Sean Parker: American entrepreneur and philanthropist (born 1979)

This Irish mathematician and physicist held Cambridge's Lucasian Professorship for an unmatched 54 years, leaving his name on equations of fluid mechanics and a theorem of vector calculus — who is it?
Sir George Stokes, 1st Baronet: British mathematician and physicist (1819–1903)
With eight legs, venom-injecting fangs, and silk-spinning spinnerets, this arthropod has spread to every continent but Antarctica — over 53,000 species and counting. What is it?
Signified by the minus sign, this arithmetic operation represents removing objects from a collection and is the inverse of addition — which operation is it?
Subtraction: One of the four basic arithmetic operations.
This daisy-family weed's yellow flowers give way to fluffy silver-tufted seed heads nicknamed 'clocks' or 'blowballs,' whose seeds scatter on the wind — which plant, better known by its common name?
Taraxacum officinale: Flowering plant species known as dandelion.
This French economist's best-selling 2013 book argued that capital returns persistently outpace economic growth, driving ever-rising wealth inequality — who is he?
This passive, energy-free process moves water through a plant and releases it as vapor from its leaves, also cooling the plant and driving nutrient flow — what is it called?
Transpiration: Process of water movement through a plant. Transpiration is the process of water movement through a plant and its evaporation from aerial parts, such as leaves, stems and flowers.
Silvery-grey and sitting at atomic number 92, this actinide has the highest atomic weight of any element that occurs naturally on Earth — and its slow decay helps date the planet itself. What is it?
Uranium: Chemical element with atomic number 92 (U)
Sold under the brand names Trintellix and Brintellix, this antidepressant belongs to a drug class called serotonin modulators and stimulators — which medication?
Vortioxetine: Serotonin modulator antidepressant. Its effectiveness is viewed as similar to that of other antidepressants.

When skin's protective barrier is broken, the body marches through a predictable sequence — hemostasis, inflammation, cell proliferation, and remodeling — to replace what was destroyed; what do we call this whole orchestrated repair process?
Wound healing: Series of events that restore integrity to damaged tissue after an injury.
Nobelium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for nobelium is No. Nobelium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol No and atomic number 102.
Nitrogen is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for nitrogen is N. Nitrogen is a chemical element; it has symbol N and atomic number 7.

Adrien Brody: Adrien Nicholas Brody (born April 14, 1973) is an American actor and visual artist.
In what year was Gordon Ramsay born?
Gordon Ramsay: Gordon James Ramsay (born (1966-11-08)8 November 1966) is a British celebrity chef, restaurateur, television presenter, and writer.
In what year was Margaret Qualley born?
Margaret Qualley: Sarah Margaret Qualley ( KWAW-lee; born October 23, 1994) is an American actress.
In what year was Sienna Miller born?
Sienna Miller: Sienna Rose Diana Miller (born 28 December 1981) is an English actress.
In what year was Wes Anderson born?
Wes Anderson: Wesley Wales Anderson (born May 1, 1969) is an American filmmaker.
In what year was Kelly Reilly born?
Kelly Reilly: Jessica Kelly Siobhán Reilly (born 18 July 1977) is an English actress.
In what year was Tom Hiddleston born?
Tom Hiddleston: Thomas William Hiddleston (born 9 February 1981) is a British actor.
In what year was Brad Pitt born?
Brad Pitt: William Bradley Pitt (born December 18, 1963) is an American actor and film producer.

Sophia Loren: Encouraged to enroll in acting lessons after entering a beauty pageant, Loren began her film career at age 16 in 1950.
In what year was Tim Curry born?
Tim Curry: Timothy James Curry (born 19 April 1946) is an English actor and singer.
In what year was Charlize Theron born?
Charlize Theron ( shar-LEEZ THERR-ən; Afrikaans: [ʃarˈlis ˈtrɔn]; born 7 August 1975) is a South African and American actress and producer.
